A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with matching title, authors, methods, and core experiments. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices support comparison; the original nine figures are retained unchanged.

before.justification: V1 reports original classification, noise-robustness, calibration, and ordinality experiments across nine datasets, including extensive appendix results.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and adds pretrained-model comparisons, inference latency measurements, and further robustness results.

M1.justification: The five classifier approaches and their loss families remain unchanged. Section 3.2 makes MLM's training template and label-probability normalization explicit without establishing a change to the implemented method. Pretrained initialization is an additional experimental setting.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same nine classification datasets and the same token-dropping and token-substitution scenarios. The pretrained comparison reuses these benchmarks; additional initialization settings, latency measurements, and degradation thresholds do not introduce new task or domain coverage.

E2.justification: The evaluated method families remain ENC, AR, ARpseudo, MLM, and DIFF. BERT-base and GPT-2 already supply the architectures in v1 Appendix B; v2's pretrained comparison changes their initialization rather than introducing another comparison method. Existing comparisons retain their participants.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 adds pretrained initialization and fine-tuning for 12-layer BERT-base ENC and GPT-2 AR across the existing sample-size grid. Appendix B introduces a separate latency protocol using batches of 1,024 sequences of length 128 on an A100. Robustness evaluation also extends to 20% and 30% F1-degradation thresholds, while the original accuracy protocols remain intact.

E4.justification: V2 adds a substantive initialization-sensitivity experiment testing whether the generative advantage survives pretraining. Tables 2–3 also quantify robustness across five degradation thresholds, whereas v1 tabulated only 10% and mentioned 5% and 15% qualitatively. Appendix G revisits scaling behavior using the retained model sizes rather than a larger-scale experiment.

E5.justification: Both versions report three random seeds and means with standard deviations. V2 introduces no changed run count, confidence-interval procedure, significance test, or uncertainty-reporting convention.

E6.justification: Figure 10 adds pretrained-model F1 curves generally favoring ENC, Table 5 adds latency measurements, and Tables 2–3 add robustness values at further thresholds. Figures 11–12 also display previously omitted one-layer ARpseudo results. The retained 12-layer DIFF token-dropping boundary at 10% F1 degradation changes from 54.4% in v1 Table 1 to 54.5% in v2 Table 2.

T1.justification: The MLM formal specification changes from conditioning on the plain input in v1 Equation 2 to the explicitly defined prompt-and-label sequence in v2 Equation 1. This is a limited correction to the documented objective. The diffusion equations and cited ELBO remain unchanged; the new bias–variance discussion supplies no new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The introduction adds pretrained-model evaluation to the stated contributions and removes its deferral to future work. The abstract, central findings from training from scratch, and conclusion's deployment recommendations otherwise retain their original meaning.

C2.justification: Section 5.1 adds an explanation for pretraining eliminating the generative low-data advantage, alongside caveats about differing objectives, corpora, architectures, and the restriction to AR and ENC. Appendix A newly attributes calibration differences to objective alignment with classification. Appendix G adds bias–variance interpretations and acknowledges that the tested scales do not demonstrate full double descent.

D1.justification: V2 adds a code-repository link, explicitly documents MLM's training suffix and normalization over label tokens, and specifies the pretrained checkpoints and latency measurement setup. Existing training hyperparameters, hardware disclosures, and training-time ranges are retained. The PDFs establish the new access information, not the repository's contents or accessibility.

R1.justification: V2 adds Geman et al. (1992), Belkin et al. (2019), and Nakkiran et al. (2019) to position the scaling discussion against bias–variance and double-descent research. It also connects the pretrained findings to Zheng et al. (2023). The original generative-versus-discriminative positioning remains intact.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main section sequence are retained. Changes comprise localized MLM clarification and editing, a new Section 5.1, and Appendices F–H for pretrained results, scaling discussion, and acknowledgments, rather than a pervasive rewrite.

P2.justification: V2 adds a qualitative comparison table, a latency table, and pretrained-result Figure 10. The robustness tables are transposed and expanded into multiple threshold columns. Figures 11–12 reorganize scaling results around model-size axes, and several floats move or resize. This substantially expands the visual presentation despite retaining Figures 1–9 unchanged.

improvement.justification: V2 usefully investigates the previously deferred pretraining question, strengthens deployment guidance with latency and fuller robustness evidence, and clarifies MLM implementation while adding a code link. These gains are tempered by incomplete integration of pretrained findings into the unchanged conclusion and a new numerical inconsistency: Table 5 implies a 600-fold DIFF/ENC latency ratio for small models, outside Appendix B's stated 20–100-fold range. The added evidence and clarification nevertheless support a limited net quality improvement.
